es-01.title: Earth System
explain: Earth science studies how the Earth was formed and how it has changed over time. It does not treat land, oceans, air, and living things separately. Instead, it views them as a single **Earth system** in which the parts influence one another. A system is a whole made of connected parts that work together.

The Earth system is usually divided into four parts.
- **Geosphere**: the solid land and rock, including everything down into the interior of the Earth.
- **Hydrosphere**: all of the Earth's water, including oceans, rivers, lakes, glaciers, and groundwater.
- **Atmosphere**: the layer of air that surrounds the Earth. Dry air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen by volume.
- **Biosphere**: the realm of living things and the living things themselves. It spans the three spheres above.

An orange arrow from the geosphere to the atmosphere is labeled volcanic gas. An arrow from the biosphere up to the atmosphere is labeled oxygen release. An arrow from the hydrosphere up to the geosphere is labeled erosion. An arrow from the hydrosphere to the biosphere is labeled water supply.

explain: The four spheres exchange matter and energy with one another. When a volcano erupts, gas and ash move from the geosphere into the atmosphere. Plants release oxygen through photosynthesis, which affects the composition of the atmosphere. Rain and rivers wear away the land and carry soil and sand to the sea. A defining feature of a system is that when one part changes, the other parts change along with it.

Two main kinds of energy drive the Earth. One is **solar energy**, which drives winds, ocean currents, and the water cycle. The other is **internal Earth energy**, the heat inside the Earth that drives volcanoes, earthquakes, and the crustal movements that build mountain ranges.

Earth's interior is layered. From the outside inward, there is the **crust**, a thin layer of rock; below it, the **mantle**, a thick layer that is mostly solid rock; then the **outer core**, which is liquid; and finally the **inner core**, which is solid. The only parts we have directly sampled are the shallow portions of the crust. The structure of the mantle and core is inferred by analyzing seismic waves.

body: When a volcano erupts, magma from the geosphere comes out onto the surface, and volcanic gas and ash spread into the atmosphere. Ash blocking sunlight can temporarily lower temperatures, and new plants grow on ground covered in ash. This is an example of a single event affecting the geosphere, atmosphere, and biosphere.

es-02.title: The Rock Cycle
explain: A **rock** is a mass formed from one or more **minerals**. A mineral is a naturally occurring solid with a definite chemical composition and crystal structure. Rocks are divided into three types according to how they formed: igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks.

An **igneous rock** forms when magma cools and solidifies. Magma is molten rock beneath the surface. When magma cools slowly deep underground, it forms a rock with large grains, and **granite** is a typical example. When it comes out onto the surface and cools quickly, it forms a rock with very small grains, and **basalt** is a typical example. The stone of Jeju Island's dolhareubang (돌하르방, traditional stone guardian statues) is basalt.

A **sedimentary rock** forms when particles such as pebbles, sand, and mud produced by weathering and erosion pile up, are compacted, and harden. **Weathering** is the breakdown and alteration of rock, and **erosion** is the wearing away and transport of broken material by water, wind, and other agents. When sand hardens, it becomes **sandstone**; when mud hardens, it becomes mudstone; and when shells and other remains of marine organisms accumulate, they form **limestone**. Sedimentary rocks form in layers and sometimes contain **fossils**. Igneous and metamorphic rocks usually pass through magma or high heat, so fossils rarely survive in them.

**Metamorphic rock** is rock whose properties have changed while it remained solid, under high heat and pressure. Limestone changes into **marble**, and rocks such as granite can change into striped **gneiss**. If the rock melts completely, it becomes magma, so that is not metamorphism.

explain.alt: Four boxes are arranged in a diamond. The top box is magma, the right box is igneous rock (granite and basalt), the bottom box is sedimentary rock (sandstone and limestone), and the left box is metamorphic rock (marble and gneiss). Orange arrows run clockwise: magma to igneous rock (cools and solidifies); igneous rock to sedimentary rock (weathering and erosion, then deposition and hardening); sedimentary rock to metamorphic rock (heat and pressure); and metamorphic rock back to magma (melts from heat). explain: As the figure shows, a rock does not stay the same once it has formed. Any rock can be weathered to become sedimentary rock, be altered by heat and pressure to become metamorphic rock, or melt to become magma. This repeating process is called the **rock cycle**. The figure shows only one path, which is simplified; in reality there are several shortcuts. For example, an igneous rock can become a metamorphic rock directly. The entire cycle takes place over very long periods of time.

examples.title: The Journey of a Grain of Sand
body: Granite on a high mountain is broken down by rain and wind into grains of sand, and a river carries them to the sea. The sand that accumulates on the seafloor is compacted by the weight of the sediment above it and hardens into sandstone. If that sandstone is buried deep underground and receives heat and pressure, it becomes metamorphic rock. A single grain can pass through all three types of rock.

es-03.title: Plate Tectonics
explain: The Earth's outer shell is not a single continuous skin but is broken into several pieces. These pieces are called **plates**. A plate is a rigid layer of rock made of the crust and the uppermost part of the mantle, and it moves slowly over the softer mantle beneath it. The theory that explains volcanoes, earthquakes, mountain ranges, and seafloor features through plate movement is called **plate tectonics**.

In the early 20th century, the German scientist Wegener proposed **continental drift**: the idea that the continents were once joined together and later separated and moved apart. The evidence included the fact that the coastlines on either side of the Atlantic fit together, that the same kinds of fossils are found on distant continents, and that traces of the same ancient glaciers line up across continents. However, he could not explain what force moved the continents, so the idea was not accepted at the time. Later, research on the seafloor revealed the movement of plates, and the theory developed into plate tectonics.

Plates move about a few centimeters each year. This is very slow, but over millions of years it adds up to enough to move continents. Plate boundaries are divided into three types depending on how the plates move.
- **Divergent boundary**: two plates move apart. Magma rises through the gap and creates new crust. The mid-ocean ridge, a long underwater mountain range, is a typical example.
- **Convergent boundary**: two plates move toward each other. When one plate sinks beneath the other (subduction), a deep ocean trench and volcanoes form; when continents collide, high mountain ranges form.
- **Transform boundary**: two plates slide past each other sideways. Crust is neither created nor destroyed here, but large earthquakes can occur.

explain: Earthquakes and volcanoes do not occur at random; they cluster near plate boundaries. This is why the area around the Pacific Ocean, with many volcanoes and earthquakes, is called the “Ring of Fire.” However, earthquakes can also occur far from plate boundaries.

es-04.title: Atmosphere and Weather
explain: The **atmosphere**, the layer of air surrounding the Earth, is divided into layers according to how its temperature changes with altitude. The lowest layer is the **troposphere**. In the troposphere, temperature decreases as altitude increases, and all weather phenomena, such as clouds, rain, and wind, occur here.

Air has weight and therefore exerts a pressure. This pressure is called **air pressure**. A place where the air pressure is higher than its surroundings is a **high-pressure area**, and a place where it is lower is a **low-pressure area**. At the center of a high-pressure area, air descends, so the weather is generally clear. At the center of a low-pressure area, air rises, which tends to form clouds and bring rain.

**Wind** is the movement of air. Air moves from areas of higher pressure to areas of lower pressure. The larger the pressure difference, the stronger the wind. Wind arises because the Earth's surface is not heated evenly.

A good example of wind direction changing within a single day occurs on the seashore. Water changes temperature more slowly than land does. So during the day, land heats up faster than the sea, and at night, land cools faster than the sea. During the day, the air over the heated land rises, so the surface on the land side becomes a low-pressure area, and a **sea breeze** blows from the sea to the land. At night the reverse happens: a **land breeze** blows from the land to the sea.

explain.alt: A cross-section of the seashore. The sea (가) is at the lower left and the land (나) is at the lower right. Near the surface, an arrow points from the sea toward the land (surface wind), and higher up, an arrow points from the land back toward the sea (upper-level wind). An orange arrow pointing up (rising) is above the land, and an orange arrow pointing down (sinking) is above the sea.

explain: How do clouds form? Air contains **water vapor**, that is, water in gaseous form. When air rises, the surrounding air pressure drops, so the air expands and its temperature falls. When the temperature drops to the point where the air can no longer hold the water vapor, namely the **dew point**, the vapor changes into water droplets. This process is called **condensation**. Droplets gather around tiny particles such as dust in the air, and this collection of droplets floating in the sky is a cloud. When the droplets grow heavy enough, they fall as rain or snow.

es-05.title: The Water Cycle and the Ocean
explain: Water on Earth does not stay in one place; it moves among the oceans, the atmosphere, and the land. This flow is called the **water cycle**. Its driving force is solar energy.

explain.alt: On the lower left is the sea, on the right is land with hills, and clouds are above. Four arrows are labeled 가, 나, 다, and 라. Arrow 가 is an orange arrow rising from the sea toward the clouds. Arrow 나 is a green arrow descending from the clouds to the land. Arrow 다 is a green arrow flowing along the land surface toward the sea. Arrow 라 is a green dotted arrow moving through the ground toward the sea.
explain.caption: The water cycle (original drawing)

explain:
The main processes of the cycle are as follows.
- **Evaporation**: water in oceans and lakes becomes water vapor and rises into the air. **Transpiration**, in which plants release water through their leaves, also adds water vapor.
- **Condensation**: rising water vapor cools and forms droplets that make up clouds.
- **Precipitation**: water in clouds falls as rain or snow.
- **Runoff**: water that lands on the ground flows along rivers to the sea. Some of it seeps into the ground and becomes **groundwater**, which slowly flows to the sea.

Most of the water on Earth is in the oceans. About 97% of all water is seawater, and the remaining 3% is **fresh water**, which has little salt. Most fresh water is locked up in glaciers and groundwater, so the water in rivers and lakes is only a very small portion.

Seawater contains dissolved substances such as salt. The amount of dissolved matter, expressed in grams per 1 kg (1000 g) of seawater, is called **salinity**, and its unit is ‰ (permille). The average salinity of the whole ocean is about 35‰. Salinity varies from region to region: seas with a lot of evaporation and little rain have high salinity, while seas into which a large amount of river water flows have low salinity. Also, even when salinity differs, the proportions of the various dissolved substances in seawater remain nearly constant.

Seawater also moves. A flow of water on the sea surface that continues in one direction is called a **surface current**, and it is driven mainly by winds. A current that flows from warm regions toward cold regions is a **warm current**, and one that flows from cold regions toward warm regions is a **cold current**. In the deep ocean, cold, salty, and therefore dense water sinks and flows slowly. Currents transport heat and help even out the Earth's climate.

body: How many grams of dissolved substances are in 2000 g of seawater with a salinity of 35‰? Since there are 35 g per 1000 g, 2000 g contains 35 × 2 = 70 g.

es-06.title: Geologic Time
explain: The history of the Earth is so long that people cannot observe it directly. So we read the records preserved in rocks, strata, and fossils to determine the order and timing of past events. The Earth is about 4.6 billion years old.

A **stratum** (layer of rock) is a layer formed by the accumulation of sediment. If there has been no deformation, the lower layer was deposited first, and the layers above it were deposited later. This is the **law of superposition**. When strata have been overturned or severely folded, this law cannot be applied directly.

Another rule is that the thing that cuts across another is younger than the thing it cuts. For example, if magma forces its way into existing rock and solidifies, forming an **intrusion**, then the intruding rock is younger than the layers it cuts through. Conversely, if an intrusion ends beneath a layer and the layer above it is continuous and unbroken, then that layer was deposited after the intrusion.

explain.alt: The figure shows a cross-section of strata (the top is the surface). Four wide layers are stacked horizontally. From top to bottom they are 라, 다, 나, and 가. An orange vertical band labeled 마 cuts vertically through layers 가, 나, and 다 and ends just below the topmost layer 라. Layer 라 is continuous and unbroken.
explain.caption: Cross-section of strata (original drawing)

explain: The method of determining only the order is called **relative age**. It tells you which is older but not how many years ago. The number of years is found using **absolute age**. Radioactive isotopes change into other elements at a constant rate over time. The time it takes for half of the original amount to change is called the **half-life**. By measuring the amount of an element remaining in a rock, one can calculate the time that has passed since the rock solidified.

Earth's history is divided into **geologic time periods** based on major events and changes in living things. From the oldest to the youngest they are the **Precambrian** (from the Earth's formation to about 540 million years ago, covering the vast majority of time), the **Paleozoic**, the **Mesozoic**, and the **Cenozoic**. In the Paleozoic, trilobites flourished and vertebrates moved from the sea onto land. In the Mesozoic, dinosaurs flourished and mostly disappeared by the end of the era. The Cenozoic is the age of mammals, and we are still in the Cenozoic. Fossils of organisms that lived only during a specific period become **index fossils**, which indicate the age of the strata in which they are found.

If the entire history of the Earth were compressed into one year, human history would appear only in the final moments of that year. Time spans far too long for people to perceive have produced the changes of the Earth.

examples.title: Finding an age from half-lives
body: Suppose an element with a half-life of 1 million years initially has 80 g. After 1 million years, 40 g remains; after 2 million years, 20 g; and after 3 million years, 10 g. After three half-lives, the amount is one-eighth of the original. If you know the remaining amount, you can count backward to determine how many half-lives have passed.

es-07.title: Magma Differentiation and Igneous Rocks
explain: Granite and basalt are both igneous rocks formed by the cooling of magma, but their colors and minerals are entirely different. Light-colored granite is abundant on the continents, while dark basalt is abundant in oceanic crust. This difference comes from **the composition of the magma from which the rock formed and how it cooled**.

Igneous rocks are classified by two criteria. **Texture** records the cooling rate. When magma cools slowly deep underground, crystals grow large, forming a **coarse-grained** (plutonic) rock; when it cools quickly at or near the surface, crystals remain small, forming a **fine-grained** (volcanic) rock. **Chemical composition** is classified by SiO₂ content. A **felsic** rock with high SiO₂ content (granite, rhyolite) is light-colored, while a **mafic** rock with low SiO₂ content (gabbro, basalt) is dark because it contains abundant iron and magnesium minerals.

Minerals do not all solidify at once as magma cools. According to the **Bowen reaction series**, established through experiments, mafic minerals such as olivine and pyroxene crystallize first at high temperatures; as the temperature falls, amphibole and biotite crystallize; and finally felsic minerals such as quartz and orthoclase crystallize. Plagioclase changes its composition continuously, from calcium-rich to sodium-rich, as the temperature decreases.

When early-crystallized mafic minerals sink and are removed from the magma, the remaining magma becomes relatively richer in SiO₂. This is called **crystal fractionation**. Through this process, increasingly felsic rock can form even from a single batch of magma. **Assimilation** of surrounding crustal rock into the magma and **mixing** of different magmas also change the composition.

The distribution of igneous rocks can be understood in connection with plate tectonics. At mid-ocean ridges and hotspots, the mantle partially melts to produce **basaltic magma**, which is mafic. At subduction zones, magma forms in mantle where water has been supplied, which lowers its melting point; as it passes through thick continental crust, it undergoes fractionation and assimilation and changes into **andesitic–rhyolitic** magma. Felsic magma is viscous and traps a lot of gas, so it tends to erupt explosively.

Limitations: the Bowen reaction series is an order under idealized experimental conditions; real magmas solidify differently depending on pressure, water content, and cooling rate. Also, “coarse-grained = plutonic” is only a tendency. Porphyritic rocks, which contain both large and small crystals, show that the cooling history had two stages.

es-08.title: Metamorphism and Geologic Structures
explain: Rocks can change without melting. When buried deep and subjected to high temperature and pressure, or brought into contact with hot magma, minerals recrystallize in the solid state and new minerals grow, producing a different rock. This is **metamorphism**. The forces a rock experiences are also recorded as **geologic structures**, such as bent and broken strata.

There are two types of metamorphism. **Contact metamorphism** occurs mainly from heat near magma and produces hard, non-directional rocks (hornfels, marble, and quartzite). **Regional metamorphism** occurs over broad areas, such as orogenic belts, under high temperature and **directed pressure** together. Platy minerals such as mica line up perpendicular to the pressure, forming **foliation**.

Regional metamorphism changes progressively with increasing intensity. As shale (mudstone) is metamorphosed more strongly, it becomes **slate → phyllite → schist → gneiss**. Slate splits into thin sheets, schist shows glittering mica, and gneiss has light and dark minerals separated into striped bands. A combination of minerals that is stable within a particular range of temperature and pressure is called a **metamorphic facies**, and from it one can work backward to estimate the conditions the rock experienced. For example, kyanite, andalusite, and sillimanite have the same chemical composition (Al₂SiO₅) but are stable at different temperatures and pressures.

When rock is subjected to force, **folds** or **faults** form. A fold is a bend in strata: if it is convex upward it is an anticline, and if it is concave downward it is a syncline. A fault is a break in strata along which they have slid. When the upper block (hanging wall) of the fault plane moves down, it is a **normal fault**, the result of **tension** pulling in opposite directions. When it moves up, it is a **reverse fault**, the result of **compressive force** pushing. When the block slides horizontally, it is a **strike-slip fault**.

Geologic structures are connected to plate boundaries. Normal faults develop at divergent boundaries (mid-ocean ridges and continental rifts), reverse faults, folds, and regional metamorphism develop at convergent boundaries (orogenic belts), and strike-slip faults develop at transform boundaries. By reading the bending and breaking of strata, one can reconstruct the plate movements that occurred in the past.

Limitations: to estimate the degree of metamorphism from pressure and temperature, one must know the original composition of the rock. Under the same conditions, shale and limestone produce completely different minerals. Also, actual strata have undergone several deformations, so their structures overlap and often cannot be explained by a single force.

Step 1: The hanging wall moved down, so it is a normal fault.

es-09.title: Radioactive Isotopes and Absolute Age
explain: We can determine from the positions of strata which of two layers is older, but not how many years ago they formed. In the early 20th century, the discovery of radioactivity revealed that rocks contain **atomic clocks** that tick at a constant rate. With them, the Earth's age was determined to be about 4.6 billion years.

A radioactive **parent element** decays into a **daughter element** with a fixed probability. The time required for the amount of the remaining parent element to halve is the **half-life**, which is hardly affected by temperature, pressure, or chemical reactions. Decay follows first-order kinetics, the same as a first-order chemical reaction, so $N = N_0(1/2)^{t/T}$. After $n$ half-lives, the parent element remains as $(1/2)^n$ and the daughter element is $1 - (1/2)^n$.

explain.alt: Horizontal axis: number of half-lives elapsed (0 to 4); vertical axis: ratio (0 to 1). The solid parent curve starts at 1 and halves with each half-life: 0.5 at 1, 0.25 at 2, and 0.125 at 3. The dashed daughter curve starts at 0 and rises to 0.5 at 1, 0.75 at 2, and 0.875 at 3.

explain: If a mineral crystallized containing only the parent element and no daughter element, the time can be found from the **parent-to-daughter ratio** measured today. A ratio of 1:1 means one half-life, 1:3 two half-lives, and 1:7 three half-lives. In general, $t = T \times \log_2\left(1 + \frac{D}{P}\right)$, where $D$ is the daughter and $P$ is the parent. The element used is chosen to match the time range to be measured. Carbon-14 (half-life about 5730 years) is used for biological remains less than tens of thousands of years old, while uranium–lead and potassium–argon series are used for rocks from millions to billions of years old.

What is being dated matters. Radiometric ages usually give the **time when the mineral solidified**, that is, when an igneous rock formed. Sedimentary rocks consist of fragments of pre-existing rocks, so they are difficult to date directly. Instead, one dates the igneous rocks above and below a sedimentary layer (lava flows, volcanic ash layers, intrusions) and uses the principle of relative dating to narrow the age range of the sedimentary layer.

Limitations: ① if the daughter element was already mixed in from the start, ② if the daughter element (especially the gas argon) later escaped, or ③ if metamorphism reset the clock, the age will be wrong. Therefore, multiple methods are cross-checked, and one checks whether the ages of different minerals from the same rock agree. Carbon-14 dates must be corrected for the fact that atmospheric carbon-14 concentration varied across different eras.

examples.title: Finding an age from a ratio
body: Condition: In a mineral, parent : daughter = 1 : 3. Half-life 1.3 billion years.
Step 1: The parent has decreased to 1/4 of its original amount, so two half-lives have passed. In the figure, this is the point where the parent is 0.25 and the daughter is 0.75.
Step 2: Age $= 2 \times 13 = 26$ (in units of 100 million years), that is, 2.6 billion years.

Interpretation: By the law of superposition, A is younger than 300 million years and older than 250 million years. The absolute ages of the igneous rocks “sandwich” the age of the sedimentary layer.

es-10.title: Air Pressure and Hydrostatic Equilibrium
explain: Climbing a high mountain makes you short of breath, and a snack bag swells up. This is because air pressure decreases as altitude increases. How air pressure falls with height is the starting point of atmospheric science.

**Air pressure** is the weight of the column of air above a point divided by the area. The average sea-level air pressure is about 1013 hPa (hectopascals). As altitude rises, less air remains above, so the pressure decreases.

Consider a thin layer of air (thickness $dz$). When the force pushing up from below and the force pressing down from above balance the weight of this layer, the air is not accelerated up or down. This balance is called **hydrostatic equilibrium**. $$\frac{dp}{dz} = -\rho g$$ The minus sign means that air pressure decreases as one goes upward. On large scales, the atmosphere is nearly always close to this equilibrium.

Air is compressible, so its density $\rho$ is not constant. Substituting the ideal gas law $\rho = \frac{p}{R_dT}$ gives $\frac{dp}{p} = -\frac{g}{R_dT}dz$, and if the temperature is constant, $$p = p_0 e^{-z/H}, \quad H = \frac{R_dT}{g}$$ where $H$ is the **scale height**, which is about 8 km in the Earth's atmosphere. Each time the altitude rises by $H$, the pressure becomes $1/e \approx 0.37$ times as large. Roughly, **pressure halves every 5.5 km**. The pressure at the summit of Mount Everest (about 8.8 km) is about one-third of the sea-level pressure.

This relationship is used in practice. Altimeters measure height using air pressure, and the **thickness between two pressure surfaces is proportional to the average temperature of the air between them** ($H \propto T$). Warm air layers are thick and cold air layers are thin. As a result, even at the same height, the pressure above a warm region becomes relatively higher, and this pressure difference creates winds (see lesson 3).

Limitations: hydrostatic equilibrium works well for large horizontal scales and slow motions, but it breaks down where vertical acceleration is large, such as in strong updrafts inside thunderstorms. Also, the exponential formula assumes that temperature is constant. The real troposphere cools with altitude, so using a mean temperature is an approximation.

examples.title: Air pressure at altitude
body: Condition: Sea-level pressure is 1000 hPa and the scale height is 8 km.
Step 1: At 8 km altitude, $1000 \times e^{-1} \approx 368$ hPa.
Step 2: At 16 km altitude, $1000 \times e^{-2} \approx 135$ hPa. Most of the mass of the atmosphere is concentrated in the lower 10 or so kilometers.

examples.title: Thickness and temperature
body: Condition: In two regions, the thickness between the 1000 hPa and 500 hPa surfaces was measured. Region A: 5.7 km; region B: 5.4 km.

Interpretation: Because thickness is proportional to mean temperature, the air column in region A is warmer. On a weather map, the boundary between cold and warm air (a front) is found from the distribution of thickness.

es-11.title: Adiabatic Lapse Rates and Atmospheric Stability
explain: On some days, cumulonimbus clouds build tall in the sky and bring showers, while on others, fog lies low and does not lift all day. The difference lies in **atmospheric stability**, that is, whether an air parcel pushed upward keeps rising or tends to return.

When an air parcel rises, the surrounding air pressure decreases, so it expands. In expanding, it does work, and its temperature falls even without any exchange of heat (an adiabatic process). The rate of temperature decrease for unsaturated air is called the **dry adiabatic lapse rate** and is about **10°C/km**. When the air becomes saturated and clouds begin to form, water vapor condenses and releases **latent heat**, which partly offsets the cooling. Therefore the **moist adiabatic lapse rate** is smaller, about **5°C/km** (4–7 depending on conditions).

explain.alt: Horizontal axis: temperature (°C, −15 to 25); vertical axis: altitude (km, 0 to 3). Three straight lines start from 20°C at the surface. ① The dry adiabatic line reaches −10°C at 3 km. ② The moist adiabatic line reaches 5°C at 3 km. ③ The surrounding atmosphere (actually measured) reaches −1°C at 3 km. At an altitude of 1 km, the three lines read 10°C, 15°C, and 13°C, respectively.

explain: Stability is judged by comparing the temperature of the air parcel with that of the **surrounding atmosphere**. The actual rate at which the temperature of the surrounding atmosphere decreases with height is called the **environmental lapse rate**. If a lifted parcel is colder (heavier) than its surroundings, it tends to sink back, which is **stable**; if it is warmer (lighter) than its surroundings, it keeps rising, which is **unstable**. Comparison rule: if the environmental lapse rate is smaller than the moist adiabatic lapse rate, the atmosphere is **absolutely stable**; if it is larger than the dry adiabatic lapse rate, it is **absolutely unstable**; if it lies between the two, it is **conditionally unstable**. A conditionally unstable atmosphere is stable when the air is unsaturated and unstable once the air becomes saturated.

The figure is an example of conditional instability. At 1 km, the surrounding atmosphere is 13°C. An unsaturated parcel follows the dry adiabatic line down to 10°C, colder than its surroundings, so it returns. A saturated parcel follows the moist adiabatic line to 15°C, warmer than its surroundings, so it keeps rising. This is why shower clouds can suddenly develop on humid summer afternoons.

Conversely, a layer in which temperature **increases with altitude**, called a **temperature inversion layer**, is very stable. On clear, calm nights the surface cools quickly, and an inversion forms near the ground, trapping fog and pollutants. Limitations: real air parcels mix with the surrounding air (entrainment) and do not follow the ideal adiabatic lines exactly. The moist adiabatic lapse rate also changes with temperature and pressure.

examples.title: Temperature of a rising air parcel and cloud height
body: Condition: Air with a surface temperature of 25°C and a dew point of 15°C rises over a mountain. For simplicity, assume that the dew point of the rising air barely changes.
Step 1: Until saturation, it cools at 10°C/km, so the height at which temperature and dew point become equal is $(25 - 15)/10 = 1$ km. Clouds form from this height.
Step 2: Above that, it cools at about 5°C/km, so at 2 km altitude it is about 10°C. (In reality, as the air rises, the dew point also gradually decreases, so the cloud base forms at about 1.2 km.)

body: Condition: Air at the top of a mountain 2 km high descends on the opposite side. It has lost moisture as rain from the clouds.

es-12.title: Geostrophic and Gradient Winds and Extratropical Cyclones
explain: We learn that wind blows from high pressure to low pressure. However, when you look at weather maps, winds at high altitude blow **parallel** to the isobars rather than across them. This is because the Earth rotates. To understand wind, we must consider the effect of rotation as well as the pressure difference.

Forces that move air: ① The **pressure gradient force** acts perpendicular to the isobars, from high pressure toward low pressure, and is stronger when the isobars are closer together. ② The **Coriolis force** (Coriolis effect) is an apparent force experienced by moving objects on the rotating Earth. It acts to the **right** of the direction of motion in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere. Its magnitude is $2\Omega\sin\varphi \cdot v$, which is larger at higher latitude $\varphi$ and greater speed $v$, and is zero at the equator.

In the upper layers (above about 1 km), where there is no surface friction, once air begins to move, the Coriolis force gradually bends the flow to the right until the **pressure gradient force and the Coriolis force are in exact opposition** and balance each other. At this point the wind blows parallel to the isobars. This is the **geostrophic wind**. In the Northern Hemisphere, if you stand with the wind at your back, **low pressure is on your left** and high pressure is on your right (Buys Ballot's law).

When isobars are curved, a **centripetal force** is also required for circular motion, and the wind in this case is called the **gradient wind**. In the Northern Hemisphere, the wind circulates counterclockwise around low pressure and clockwise around high pressure. Near the ground, **friction** slows the wind and weakens the Coriolis force, so the wind crosses the isobars at an angle and flows into low pressure. Thus air converges at the center of a low and **rises**, forming clouds and rain, while at the center of a high it **sinks** and the weather is clear.

The main character of mid-latitude weather is the **extratropical cyclone**. It develops at **fronts** where cold and warm air meet. In front of a **warm front**, where warm air gently rides up over cold air, broad stratiform clouds and persistent rain form. Near a **cold front**, where cold air wedges under warm air, narrow, strong cumulus clouds and showers form. When the cold front moves faster and catches up with the warm front, it becomes an **occluded front**, and the cyclone weakens. Extratropical cyclones help transport and mix heat between the south and north.

Limitations: the geostrophic wind is an ideal state with no friction and straight flow. Near the equator, the Coriolis force is almost zero, so the concept of geostrophic wind cannot be used; for this reason, typhoons do not form directly over the equator. The geostrophic balance is a good approximation of large-scale flow, but changes in weather arise from small **deviations** from this balance.

examples.title: Reading wind direction on a weather map
body: Condition: Northern Hemisphere, isobars running east–west, with low pressure to the north and high pressure to the south. Upper layer.
Step 1: The pressure gradient force points north. The geostrophic wind is perpendicular to it, and with the wind at your back, the low pressure (north) must be on your left.
Step 2: Therefore the wind blows from west to east (a westerly). This matches the westerlies that blow in the upper mid-latitudes.

examples.title: Interpreting a record of a front passing
body: Condition: At an observing station over one day, the pressure fell and then rose again, the temperature suddenly dropped by 5°C, a short, intense shower fell, and the wind shifted from southwesterly to northwesterly.
Interpretation: A cold front passed. Cold air moved in, causing a sharp drop in temperature, and the cumulus clouds of the front produced the shower.

checks.hint: With the wind at your back, the low pressure must be on your left.
checks.explanation: Facing north, the left is west (low pressure) and the right is east (high pressure), so the wind is a south wind.

es-13.title: Temperature–Salinity Diagrams and Water Masses
explain: The ocean looks like a single body of water, but in fact **water masses** with different properties form layers and move slowly. Each water mass carries a “fingerprint” of the temperature and salinity of the place where it formed and travels thousands of kilometers. Oceanographers read these fingerprints to trace the origin and path of seawater.

Seawater **density** is determined mainly by **temperature** and **salinity**. Colder water and saltier water are denser. Temperature changes through heating and cooling at the sea surface; salinity changes through evaporation (which raises it), precipitation and river inflow (which lowers it), and sea ice formation (which raises it, because salt is expelled into the surrounding water as ice forms). Denser water sinks and spreads beneath lighter water.

explain.alt: A temperature–salinity diagram with salinity (psu, 33.5 to 36.5) on the horizontal axis and temperature (°C, 0 to 25) on the vertical axis. Three dotted lines rising diagonally to the right are lines of equal density, and the label says density increases toward the lower right. Water mass A is plotted at salinity 36 and temperature 20°C, water mass B at salinity 34.5 and temperature 4°C, and water mass C at salinity 35 and temperature 2°C.

explain: A **temperature–salinity diagram** (T-S diagram) places salinity on the horizontal axis and temperature on the vertical axis. By drawing **isopycnals** (lines of equal density) on it, one can compare the densities of different waters at a glance. As in the figure, density increases toward the lower right (salty and cold). The isopycnals are curved because the effect of temperature on density depends on the temperature itself; in cold water, the effect of temperature changes is smaller.

What can be done with a T-S diagram? ① **Water mass identification**: when the temperature and salinity measured at different depths at one observation point are plotted, different water masses appear as corners of the bent curve. ② **Mixing tracing**: when two water masses mix, the mixed water lies on the straight line connecting the two points, and its position gives the mixing ratio. ③ **Stability assessment**: if water above is denser than water below, the arrangement is unstable and overturns (convection).

An interesting result is **density increase by mixing**. Because the isopycnals are curved, when two water masses of the same density are mixed, the mixture can become **slightly denser** than either of the two. This effect contributes to the formation of deep water. Limitations: the density in a T-S diagram is referenced to surface pressure, so when comparing very deep waters, a density corrected for pressure effects must be used.

es-14.title: Ekman Transport, Coastal Upwelling, and Western Intensification
explain: One might expect that when wind pushes the sea surface, seawater flows in the direction of the wind. However, in the late 19th century, the Arctic explorer Nansen observed that icebergs drifted not in the direction of the wind but to its **right**. Ekman solved this puzzle through the effect of the Earth's rotation.

When wind drags the surface seawater, the Coriolis force (covered in stage 3) bends the flow to the right in the Northern Hemisphere. Surface water flows at about 45° to the right of the wind, and the layer beneath is pulled along by the layer above, flowing further right and more slowly. This spiral pattern, in which the flow direction rotates with depth, is called the **Ekman spiral**. The net transport of the whole layer affected by the wind is to the **right of the wind direction** (in the Northern Hemisphere). This is the **Ekman transport**. In the Southern Hemisphere, it is to the left.

explain.alt: A map of a Northern Hemisphere coast (north at the top). The left side is sea and the right side is land, with a vertical coastline between them. Over the sea, a wind arrow runs parallel to the coast from north to south. The label reads “Net transport of surface seawater = ?”

explain: When Ekman transport is directed away from the coast, surface water moves away from the shore, and cold, nutrient-rich water from the depths rises to fill the gap. This is **coastal upwelling**. Conversely, when Ekman transport is directed toward the coast, surface water piles up and sinks, a process called **downwelling**. Upwelling zones have abundant plankton because of their nutrients and become world-class fishing grounds. In the Northern Hemisphere, a north wind (blowing toward the south) that runs parallel to a coast with the sea to the west and land to the east, as in the figure, causes upwelling.

At the scale of an ocean basin, the Ekman transport driven by the trade winds and the westerlies gathers water toward the center of the subtropical gyre, slightly raising the sea surface there. The balance between this slope and the Coriolis force creates a large **gyre** (a circulating system of currents). However, the flow of the gyre is not symmetric east to west: it is **narrow, fast, and deep at the western edge of the ocean** (the Kuroshio and the Gulf Stream). This is called **western intensification**, and it arises from the effect in which the strength of the Coriolis force varies with latitude (the $\beta$ effect). Currents on the eastern edge are broad and slow.

Limitations: Ekman's theory assumes that the sea is infinitely deep, that the wind blows steadily for a long time, and that friction is simple. In real shallow seas, or where the wind changes often, the direction of transport appears at an angle smaller than 90°. Also, at the equator the Coriolis force is zero, so the theory cannot be applied directly there.

es-15.title: Thermohaline Circulation: The Global Conveyor Belt
explain: Surface currents are created by the wind, but the deep water that makes up most of the ocean does not feel the wind directly. That deep water also moves very slowly. The driving force is **density differences**, that is, differences in temperature (heat) and salinity (salt). For this reason, this circulation is called the **thermohaline circulation**.

Deep water forms in polar seas. In winter, surface water is strongly cooled in places such as the North Atlantic near Greenland and the Weddell Sea in Antarctica, and the salt expelled as sea ice forms adds further to its density, which becomes very high. This water sinks to the bottom and becomes **deep water**. Water that sinks in the North Atlantic becomes North Atlantic Deep Water, and water that sinks around Antarctica becomes Antarctic Bottom Water. Antarctic Bottom Water is the densest and lies at the very bottom.

Sinking deep water spreads southward along the ocean floor and then into the Indian and Pacific Oceans. There it slowly mixes, warms, and rises, and then returns to the North Atlantic along surface currents. This global path is often compared to a **conveyor belt**. A single circuit takes on the order of **a thousand years**.

Thermohaline circulation strongly affects climate. The flow that draws warm surface water into the North Atlantic helps make northwestern Europe milder than other regions at the same latitude. It also carries carbon dioxide and oxygen from the surface down to the deep sea, storing atmospheric carbon in the ocean for long periods.

This circulation is sensitive to surface density. If large amounts of meltwater from glaciers flow into the polar seas, surface salinity drops, the water does not become dense enough, and its tendency to sink may weaken. Paleoclimate records show traces of such weakening in the past, accompanied by abrupt climate change. How much and how quickly the present circulation may weaken is still being studied, and projections are highly uncertain.

Limitations: the “conveyor belt” is a simplification to aid understanding. The real deep circulation is not a single belt but a complicated flow of many eddies and intertwined paths, and mixing by wind and tides also plays an important role in lifting water upward. Explaining the circulation by density differences alone is only half of the picture.

es-16.title: Radiative Equilibrium and the Greenhouse Effect
explain: The Earth continuously receives energy from the Sun. Yet the Earth does not keep getting hotter and maintains a fairly constant temperature, because it radiates back to space as much energy as it receives. The state in which incoming and outgoing energy are equal is called **radiative equilibrium**. This simple balance allows a first approximation of the Earth's temperature.

Outside the Earth's atmosphere, solar radiation is about $S = 1361$ W/m² (the solar constant). The Earth intercepts sunlight over its cross-sectional area $\pi R^2$, but it radiates energy from its entire surface area $4\pi R^2$. Dividing by the surface area gives an average of $S/4 \approx 340$ W/m². About 30% of this is reflected back by clouds, ice, and the surface and leaves immediately. This fraction is called the **reflectance (albedo)** $\alpha \approx 0.3$. The absorbed amount is $(1 - \alpha)S/4 \approx 238$ W/m².

A body radiates depending on its temperature; a blackbody radiates $\sigma T^4$ per unit area (the Stefan–Boltzmann law, $\sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8}$). Setting absorption equal to emission, $$\sigma T_e^4 = \frac{(1 - \alpha)S}{4}$$ gives an **effective radiating temperature** $T_e \approx 255$ K, about $-18$°C. However, the actual average surface temperature is about 288 K (15°C). This **33 K difference** is the greenhouse effect.

Solar radiation is mainly visible light, which passes easily through the atmosphere, but the radiation emitted by the surface is infrared. **Greenhouse gases** such as water vapor, carbon dioxide, and methane absorb infrared radiation and re-emit it in all directions, sending part of it back down to the surface. The surface therefore receives more energy than it would without the atmosphere and becomes warmer. Seen from space, the Earth still emits as if at 255 K, but that radiation comes mainly from the **upper atmosphere**.

Let us understand the greenhouse effect with a simple model. Place one atmospheric layer that absorbs all infrared radiation above the surface. The atmospheric layer emits the same amount upward and downward, so the surface receives both the absorbed solar energy and the downward radiation from the atmosphere. Calculated this way, the surface temperature is $2^{1/4}T_e \approx 303$ K. That this is higher than the actual value (288 K) is because the real atmosphere absorbs only part of the infrared, and convection carries heat upward. The simple model shows the **direction and principle** rather than the exact value.

Limitations: this calculation treats the Earth as a single point and deals only with averages. In reality, there are large differences by latitude, day and night, and season, and those differences drive atmospheric and oceanic circulation. Also, albedo and greenhouse gas concentrations change along with the climate. This is the climate feedback covered in the next lesson.

es-17.title: Climate Feedbacks and El Niño–Southern Oscillation
explain: When a small change occurs in the climate system, that change alters other factors, and those in turn either amplify or dampen the original change. Such a loop is called **feedback**. How sensitively the climate responds to a change is determined mostly by feedbacks. The climate also oscillates on its own without any external change, and the best-known example is **El Niño**.

**Positive feedback** (amplifies the change): ① **Ice–albedo feedback**: when the temperature rises, ice and snow decrease, reducing the albedo; more sunlight is absorbed, and the planet becomes warmer still. ② **Water vapor feedback**: warmer air can hold more water vapor, and water vapor is a strong greenhouse gas, which amplifies the warming. For each 1°C of warming, the atmosphere can hold about 7% more water vapor.

**Negative feedback** (dampens the change): the most fundamental one is **radiative feedback**. As the Earth warms, the radiation emitted to space increases according to $\sigma T^4$, so the planet cools. Clouds can act in both directions. Low clouds reflect sunlight and have a cooling effect, while high thin clouds trap infrared radiation and have a large warming effect. Cloud feedback is one of the largest sources of uncertainty in climate projections.

**El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO)** is a natural variation produced jointly by the atmosphere and ocean of the tropical Pacific. Normally, the trade winds blow from east to west, piling warm surface water in the western Pacific, while in the eastern Pacific (along South America), cold water rises through upwelling (stage 4). During **El Niño**, the trade winds weaken, warm water spreads eastward, and upwelling in the eastern Pacific weakens, so sea surface temperatures rise above normal. The rain clouds also shift eastward, changing precipitation patterns in many parts of the world. The opposite state, in which the trade winds strengthen, is **La Niña**.

ENSO itself contains feedback. When the eastern Pacific warms, the east–west temperature difference shrinks, the trade winds weaken further, and when the trade winds weaken, the eastern Pacific warms even more (a positive feedback, the Bjerknes feedback). This amplification ends as slow waves in the ocean's interior return the state, and it repeats roughly every 2 to 7 years. The name ENSO reflects the discovery that the atmospheric pressure oscillation (the **Southern Oscillation**) and the ocean temperature change (**El Niño**) are two faces of the same phenomenon.

Limitations: it is difficult to measure the magnitude of feedbacks accurately, and cloud and carbon cycle feedbacks in particular have large uncertainties. ENSO also does not have a constant period, and each event has a different shape. How long-term climate change interacts with ENSO is still under study.

es-18.title: Paleoclimate Proxies: Reading the Past Climate
explain: Temperature records from thermometers extend back only a few hundred years at most. How do we know the climate of earlier times, when ice ages and interglacial periods alternated over hundreds of thousands of years? Nature holds **proxies** (stand-in indicators) that record past climate indirectly. Paleoclimatology reads these records and examines the limits of their interpretation.

Representative proxies include: ① **Ice cores**: the annual layers of snow accumulated on Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets preserve records spanning hundreds of thousands of years. **Air bubbles** trapped in the ice hold the atmosphere of the time, so carbon dioxide and methane concentrations can be measured directly. ② **Marine sediments**: the chemical composition and species of plankton shells record water temperature and ice volume. ③ **Tree rings**, **corals**, **cave deposits**, and **pollen**: these record growing conditions year by year or layer by layer.

The most widely used proxy is the **oxygen isotope ratio**. Oxygen has the light ¹⁶O and the heavy ¹⁸O. When water evaporates, the lighter ¹⁶O evaporates more easily, and as vapor travels and falls as rain or snow, the heavier ¹⁸O is removed first. Therefore, snow at the poles contains less ¹⁸O. In colder periods this effect is stronger, so the **¹⁸O ratio in glacier ice becomes lower**. The ¹⁸O ratio of an ice core reflects the local temperature.

Records from the **ocean** are read in the opposite direction. During glacial periods, water rich in ¹⁶O becomes trapped in the huge continental ice sheets, so the remaining seawater becomes **relatively richer in ¹⁸O**. Plankton shells (calcium carbonate) record the ratio of the surrounding water, so layers with a high ¹⁸O ratio in marine sediments indicate times when the ice sheets were large, that is, glacial periods. The key point is that the same isotope responds in opposite directions depending on where it is recorded.

These records show that over the past roughly 800,000 years, glacial and interglacial periods repeated at intervals of about 100,000 years, and that carbon dioxide concentration and temperature varied closely together. The glacial cycle is understood as being triggered by subtle changes in Earth's orbit (eccentricity, axial tilt, and precession) that alter the distribution of insolation, the **Milankovitch cycles**, and amplified by carbon dioxide and ice–albedo feedbacks.

Limitations: proxies do not measure temperature **directly**; they are also affected by other factors. Tree-ring width responds to precipitation as well as temperature, and isotope ratios change when the source of water vapor shifts. Dating also has errors. Therefore, multiple proxies are cross-checked, and interpretation is done after calibration against modern observations.

checks.prompt: In two or three sentences, explain why the ¹⁸O signals in ice cores and marine sediments show opposite trends during glacial periods.
checks.hint: Follow the path of water (ocean → atmosphere → ice sheet).

checks.model: Lighter ¹⁶O evaporates more readily and travels to the poles, so polar snow and glacier ice contain less ¹⁸O, and the colder it is, the less they contain. During glacial periods, water rich in ¹⁶O is trapped in huge ice sheets, so the remaining seawater becomes relatively richer in ¹⁸O. Thus the ¹⁸O in glacier ice falls, while the ¹⁸O in marine sediments rises.

es-19.title: Integrated Problem Solving: Tracing the Earth's Energy Budget
explain: The first capstone lesson traces, as a single flow, how the solar energy that reaches the Earth **passes through the geosphere, atmosphere, and hydrosphere and then leaves for space**. Atmospheric stability, ocean circulation, radiative equilibrium, and feedbacks, which were learned separately in stages 2 through 5, are connected in one scene.

**Stage 1 (global budget)**: of the average 340 W/m² incoming at the top of the atmosphere, about 100 is reflected and about 240 is absorbed. Of the absorbed amount, about 160 is absorbed by the surface and about 80 by the atmosphere. At equilibrium, the infrared radiation leaving to space is also about 240. The surface passes the energy it receives to the atmosphere not only through infrared radiation but also through **sensible heat** (directly warming the air) and **latent heat** (evaporating water). The latent heat, about 80 W/m², is the fuel that warms the atmosphere when the condensation latent heat covered in stage 3 is released.

**Stage 2 (latitudinal imbalance)**: the tropics receive more incoming solar energy than they radiate as infrared, and the poles do the reverse. Yet the tropics do not keep getting hotter, because the atmosphere and oceans **carry heat toward the poles**. In the atmosphere, the Hadley circulation and extratropical cyclones (stage 3) do this work, and in the ocean, western boundary currents and the thermohaline circulation (stage 4) do it. Most of the heat transport occurs in the atmosphere at mid-latitudes, while in low latitudes the ocean's share is large.

**Stage 3 (disturbance and response)**: when greenhouse gas concentrations rise, the infrared radiation escaping to space temporarily decreases, creating a **radiative imbalance** (forcing). The Earth stores more energy and warms, and as temperature rises, emission by $\sigma T^4$ increases until balance is restored. During this process, water vapor and ice–albedo feedbacks (stage 5) amplify the change. Most of the surplus energy absorbed (about 90%) is stored in the **ocean**, which has a large heat capacity, so the temperature response appears later than the forcing.

**Stage 4 (verification)**: we check such reasoning against data. Satellites measure the incoming and outgoing radiation at the top of the atmosphere, and ocean observation buoys measure water temperature down to depths of thousands of meters to calculate the heat stored in the ocean. Paleoclimate proxies (stage 5) show that carbon dioxide and temperature changed together in the past. The essence of geoscientific reasoning is to see whether independent lines of evidence point to the same conclusion.

**Critique**: a global mean budget erases regional differences and seasonal changes. Also, the numbers can differ by several W/m² depending on the observation method, and since this small imbalance (on the order of 1 W/m²) is at the core of climate change, measurement accuracy is extremely important. A view that appreciates both the simplicity of the average and the complexity of the details is needed.

examples.title: Balancing the surface energy budget
body: Condition (approximate): The surface receives 160 from solar absorption and 340 from atmospheric back-radiation. The surface emits 398 of infrared, 20 of sensible heat, and 82 of latent heat.
Step 1: Total received 500, total emitted 500.

Step 2: Solving the surface infrared emission of 398 W/m² with $\sigma T^4$ gives $T \approx 289$ K, which matches the mean surface temperature. The fact that atmospheric back-radiation exceeds solar absorption is the essence of the greenhouse effect.

examples.title: Delay caused by the ocean
body: Condition: A 1 m² column of ocean in a 100 m deep mixed layer (about $10^5$ kg of water, specific heat 4000 J/(kg·K)) accumulates an imbalance of 1 W/m² for one year.
Step 1: One year $\approx 3.15 \times 10^7$ s, so the accumulated energy $\approx 3.15 \times 10^7$ J.
Step 2: $\Delta T = 3.15 \times 10^7/(10^5 \times 4000) \approx 0.08$ K. Because of the ocean's large heat capacity, the response is slow.

es-20.title: Bachelor's Capstone: Analyzing and Critiquing an Earth System Phenomenon
explain: The final task is to **choose one Earth system phenomenon, analyze it through the interactions of the geosphere, atmosphere, and hydrosphere (and the biosphere where needed), and critique the data used and the limits of their interpretation**. Examples include summer heavy rainfall in a region, fluctuations in coastal upwelling fisheries, the effect of volcanic eruptions on climate, terrain prone to landslides, and sea-level change.

Analytical framework: ① **Define the phenomenon**: what, when, where, and how much. ② **Relevant spheres and processes**: for example, for heavy rain, the ocean (water vapor supply), the atmosphere (stability, low-pressure systems, fronts), and the terrain (forced uplift by mountains). ③ **Flows of energy and matter**: where do heat, water, and carbon come from, and where do they go? ④ **Feedbacks and timescales**: is the change on a daily, seasonal, decadal, or geologic scale? ⑤ **Evidence**: what will you use to confirm it, such as observations (weather, ocean, satellite), geologic records, or proxies?

Questions for critique: Are the spatial and temporal resolutions of the data sufficient to capture the phenomenon? Can a record from one location be generalized to a wide area? Has a correlation been interpreted as causation? Has natural variability (such as El Niño) been distinguished from the long-term trend? Because Earth science data often cannot be produced by repeating experiments, agreement among multiple independent lines of evidence is especially important.

This lesson is not a guideline for disaster response or safety decisions. Actual judgments about disaster risk should follow the official information from the relevant agencies. The task is not graded, and submitted writing is stored only on this device and can be viewed again under 'My notes' in 'My progress'.

examples.title: Model structure: heavy rainfall on a mountain's windward side
body: Phenomenon: In summer, rain concentrates on the southern slope of a mountain range.

Process: Water vapor evaporated from the warm sea (storing latent heat) → a southerly wind climbs the mountain and cools adiabatically → after saturation it cools at the moist adiabatic rate; if conditionally unstable, cumulonimbus clouds develop → the latent heat of condensation further strengthens the rising motion (positive feedback) → the opposite slope is dry because of the Föhn effect.
Evidence: Rainfall observations by slope, radar, and upper-air temperature observations to confirm the stability.
Critique: If observation stations are concentrated in valleys, rainfall at the mountain summit may be underestimated.

examples.title: Model structure: a large volcanic eruption and climate
body: Process: Sulfur dioxide carried into the stratosphere by an eruption becomes sulfate aerosols that reflect sunlight → albedo increases → the surface cools for one to two years.
Evidence: Global temperature observations after the eruption, and sulfate layers in ice cores.
Critique: Natural variability occurring at the same time, such as El Niño, may mask or exaggerate the cooling effect, so it must be considered together.

checks.model: The phenomenon to analyze is heavy snowfall on the western coast in winter. Cold, dry air from Siberia (atmosphere) passes over the relatively warm Yellow Sea (ocean) and receives heat and water vapor, so the lower layer becomes unstable. When this air meets the coastal terrain (geosphere), it is forced upward, cools adiabatically, and snow clouds develop. The larger the temperature difference between the sea and the air, the more heat and water vapor are supplied, and the more snow falls.
